spec_notes: No contradiction of the request. The spec marks three of its own choices as 'Default of 2026-11-22': repeated names collapse to one member in first-listed order (U-6), HTTP amounts must be safe integers (cents above 2^53-1 rejected, a limit the request does not set), and one Node process owns each DATA_FILE. It decides without marking that rejected expenses do not consume an index, that 404 precedes body validation (R-5), that share values must be valid (negative/fractional rejected), and that a fresh file begins empty. It is silent on balances summing to 0, the {from,to,cents} shape of a payment, payments bringing balances to zero, invalid JSON bodies, a corrupt DATA_FILE, and crash safety (the temp-file-and-rename choice is only in architecture.md AD-1). R-6 carries a test result line ('24 concurrent writes survived restart') inside a requirement. The 34/33/33 example pins the remainder rule by example only.
tests_notes: Six tests each cover many behaviours: TC-1 mixes group validation, 409, empty balances/settlements and all 404 routes; TC-3 loops over ~20 invalid bodies built from one exact-split template, so the cents checks are masked by the share-sum check: weakening cents <= 0 to < 0 (S-22) or replacing Number.isSafeInteger with a number type check (S-23) leaves all six passing. The fixture depends on the server printing exactly 'Listening on port N' on stdout and honouring PORT=0, so another correct build that prints differently or logs elsewhere would fail every test; a server ignoring PORT but printing its real port would pass. TC-1's de-duplication check uses zero balances, which would not notice a member counted twice. TC-5 is the only concurrency and restart test (24 requests). Nothing tests crash safety, corrupt files, group-creation races, aborted bodies or that GETs are read-only.
maintainer: Correctness under concurrency rests on an unstated invariant: after the asynchronous body read, validation, the synchronous writeFileSync+renameSync and the in-memory state swap all happen with no await in between; adding any async step (async fs, a lock, logging) there would silently allow lost or duplicated expenses, and only TC-5's 24-request race would have a chance to notice. Balances and settlements are emitted as hand-built JSON strings from BigInts, so changing the response shape means editing string templates where escaping or syntax mistakes are easy. Each write rewrites the whole file, which is fine at this scale but is the first thing to change if data grows.
